comment_text.value:
We've seen many open source software libraries, frameworks, and hosting platforms with vulnerabilities, backdoors, or leaks.

In my opinion, to suggest open-weight models are extensively analyzed while being net new and continuously released and the model itself being unintelligible to humans seems a bit premature.

It's possible that closed-weight models end up following the pattern of being arguably less secure since there are fewer eyes on them analogous to open source software but I don't think there's a perfect match here.

comment_text.value: Backdoors in model weights are mostly theoretical. And the "alignment problem" that the AI labs love to talk about really doesn't exist either, at least, not the way they use it. The real alignment problem is getting an LLM, which is just math, to obey arbitrary human rules. In other words, LLMs do not have "alignment" at all. However, AI CEOs abuse the term and use it to mean "AI has an alignment, just not the one we want".

comment_text.value:
> Paid models have an incentive not to do that because if the market discovers it there is a huge economy penalty, but the free open source models don't have that disincentive.

This just fundamentally isn't true. They run on the same economic model, but they have to release the weights to gain credibility, unlike the American labs.

> Do you ever worry whether these open source models have been trained to embed backdoors or leak secrets in very specific circumstances at some point in the future?

Open weight models are extensively analyzed. It is extremely unlikely there is an intentional 'backdoor when X' concept added to any of them. Not impossible, but unlikely for the same economic incentives you see in the other labs, and given that no evidence of anything along those lines has surfaced yet.

comment_text.value:
>There are zero reasons to have any less concerns about ideological biases, side effects of the mechanisms used to implement ideological biases, or code backdoors in a US model

If you are a US based critical infrastructure provider, I'd argue that you have already accepted a baked-in threat of ideological misalignment from the US, but you have not accepted it from farther away countries like China.

>a supplier of open (as opposed to hosted) model weights is not an active ongoing partner with whom the idea of supply chain risk from possible future divergence of interests is coherent

I disagree. Models are improving so quickly that you'd probably not want to freeze yourself on an older model forever. You likely want to continue to upgrade models. The best way to do this is to build a sufficiently powerful and representative benchmark that you can confidently move to _any_ model, but you might expect that future models from the same providers that you accepted before will show less divergence than totally new providers. Similarly, if you build your inference around one of their custom tools (e.g. DeepInfer rather than vLLM), you might find substantial switching costs in moving away to another provider.

>And your speculation about future protectionist regulation is just that, not an actual fact.

It's not a done deal for sure, but you can already see a lot of signs of this in recent actions from the government. I can tell you based on personal experience that some customers will automatically rule out any Chinese models.

comment_text.value:
There are a number of reasons that you might not want to build your inference stack on a Chinese origin model even if you're running it entirely in house.

For one, you might not trust that the weights do not contain ideological biases (e.g. ask DeepSeek about tibet) or that the methods used to impose these biases may not have contaminated the model in some other way.

For another, you might not trust that the code the model generates won't be backdoored or attempt to leak information through your sandboxes.

For a third, you may not want to build your stack on a partner who you feel is a supply chain risk, who might become unaligned with your interests.

By far the biggest though, is that many industries will be forbidden from doing so by the government in an attempt to protect the US model industry (and thus create the demand for some model like this one).

I'm always excited to see new entrants to this open-models race, no matter why they're running.
